title: IFCN Code of Principles (International Fact-Checking Network)

extracted.subtask_short: Auditing rigor of a claim-evidence match/verdict
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing whether a claim-verification decision (match/no-match, true/false) was reached with a consistent evidentiary standard, sourced transparently from named/primary evidence, and weighing both supporting and undermining evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Same standard of evidence and judgement for equivalent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Signatory organizations must fact-check claims using "the same standard of evidence and judgement for equivalent claims" regardless of who makes the claim or what position it supports — not concentrating fact-checking efforts on any one side of a debate, following the same verification process for every single fact-check, and letting the evidence — not the fact-checker's own views — dictate the conclusion reached.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose conflicts of interest affecting claim assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclosing any conflicts of interest, in sources used or in the fact-checking organization's own affiliations, that could color the assessment of a claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide enough information for readers to replicate the work
rubrics_metrics.description: Signatories must provide "enough information for readers to be able to replicate their work themselves" — meaning every fact-check must disclose exactly which sources were consulted, not merely assert a conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize primary sources over secondary reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize primary sources over secondary reporting on those sources — e.g., a government dataset over a news article citing the dataset, an original court filing over a summary of the filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verify key claim elements against more than one named source
rubrics_metrics.description: Verify the key elements of a claim against more than one named source whenever more than one relevant, independent source exists. Single-sourcing is acceptable only when no second source is available, and this limitation should be disclosed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Name sources rather than relying on vague attribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Name sources whenever it is safe and ethical to do so, rather than relying on unnamed or vague attribution ("experts say"), so that the reader (or a downstream auditor) can independently check the chain of evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Disclose evidentiary gaps rather than smoothing them over
rubrics_metrics.description: Disclose when a source could not be reached for comment or when the claimant refused to provide substantiating evidence — an evidentiary gap must be surfaced, not silently smoothed over.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present both corroborating and contradicting evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Present relevant evidence that appears to support the claim as well as relevant evidence that appears to undermine it — i.e., an explicit accounting of both corroborating and contradicting evidence, rather than a one-sided presentation optimized to justify the final verdict. This is a direct instruction against selectively reporting only the evidence that fits a predetermined rating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish checking a literal statement vs. the impression it leaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Make clear whether the piece is checking a literal statement, or the impression/gist that a statement leaves, since these can require different evidentiary standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open and transparent correction reaching the original audience
rubrics_metrics.description: When an error is found, the organization must correct it "openly and transparently, seeking as far as possible to ensure that users of the original see the correction" — a correction is not complete merely because a private edit was made. The correction should explain what was wrong, why, and what has changed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five-question checklist for auditing a claim-matching decision
rubrics_metrics.description: The Code implies a fact-checker should be able to answer, for any claim-evidence pair under evaluation: (1) Was the same evidentiary bar applied here as would be applied to a claim on the "other side"? (2) Which sources were consulted, are they named, and is at least one of them primary? (3) Was more than one independent source used to corroborate the key factual element, where more than one existed? (4) Does the resulting verdict explicitly weigh both supporting and undermining evidence, rather than cherry-picking? (5) Is the reasoning chain transparent enough that an outside party could replicate the check and arrive at the same verdict?
